pages.title: Part 1: Exercise Types: Core, Assistance, Structural, and Power Exercises
pages.readingHtml:
Taxonomy of Resistance Training Exercises

Exercise selection constitutes Step 2 of designing an athletic resistance training program. Although there are hundreds of available movements, exercises are categorized based on their relative importance to sport performance, the magnitude of muscle mass involved, joint kinematics, and postural axial loading.

Core versus Assistance Exercises

Exercises are primarily classified into two fundamental categories based on muscle mass recruitment and multi-joint complexity:

  • Core Exercises: Recruit one or more large muscle areas (e.g., chest, shoulder, back, hip, or thigh) and involve two or more primary joints (multijoint exercises). Because core exercises engage extensive muscle mass and allow heavy loading, they receive primary priority when selecting exercises due to their direct transfer to athletic performance. Examples include the back squat, bench press, deadlift, and power clean.
  • Assistance Exercises: Recruit smaller muscle areas (e.g., upper arm, abdominal muscles, calf, neck, forearm, lower back, or anterior lower leg) and involve only one primary joint (single-joint exercises). Assistance exercises are considered secondary for direct sport performance enhancements but play a critical role in injury prevention, tissue reconditioning, and targeting isolated muscular deficits. Examples include the leg (knee) extension, arm (biceps) curl, and lateral shoulder raise.
Anatomical Joint Conventions in Resistance Training

When categorizing exercises as single-joint or multi-joint, specific anatomical anatomical complexes are treated as single primary joints:

  • Shoulder Complex: All articulations of the shoulder (including the glenohumeral joint and shoulder girdle) are collectively treated as a single primary joint. Thus, an exercise like the dumbbell lateral raise is classified as a single-joint assistance exercise.
  • Spinal Column: The vertebral column is similarly treated as a single primary joint for exercises such as abdominal crunches or back extensions.

Clinical and Preventative Applications of Assistance Exercises

A primary application of assistance exercises is in prehabilitation (injury prevention) and rehabilitation. By isolating specific muscles that undergo high repetitive stress during sport skills, strength and conditioning professionals can reinforce vulnerable joints. For example, overhand baseball pitchers undergo extreme eccentric decelerative stress on the posterior shoulder; prescribing assistance exercises for the shoulder external rotators (e.g., dumbbell external rotation) stabilizes the glenohumeral joint. Similarly, following muscle contusions or strain (e.g., a quadriceps contusion), targeted single-joint assistance lifts enable controlled reconditioning of damaged motor units.

Structural and Power Exercises

Core multijoint exercises can be further sub-classified based on axial spinal loading and movement velocity:

  • Structural Exercises: A core exercise that loads the spine directly (e.g., back squat) or indirectly (e.g., power clean) is classified as a structural exercise. Structural movements demand active muscular stabilization of posture, requiring the athlete to maintain a rigid torso and neutral spine under load.
  • Power Exercises: A structural exercise executed very quickly or explosively is classified as a power exercise. Power exercises (e.g., power clean, snatch, push jerk) require rapid rate of force development ($\text{RFD}$) and high mechanical power output ($P = \text{Force} \times \text{Velocity}$), making them essential for sports requiring jump, sprint, or throw acceleration.
Exercise Category Muscle Mass Involved Primary Joints Involved Spinal Loading Execution Velocity Primary Utility in Program Design
Core Exercises Large (Chest, Hip, Thigh, Back) Multijoint ($\ge 2$ Joints) Variable (Direct/Indirect/None) Controlled to Moderate Primary sport performance & maximal strength
Assistance Exercises Small (Arm, Calf, Neck, Abdomen) Single-Joint ($1$ Joint) Minimal / None Controlled Prehabilitation, rehab, & muscle isolation
Structural Exercises Large (Full Kinetic Chain) Multijoint ($\ge 2$ Joints) Direct or Indirect Axial Load Controlled to Moderate Core stability, posture, & axial force transfer
Power Exercises Large (Full Kinetic Chain) Multijoint ($\ge 2$ Joints) Direct or Indirect Axial Load Explosive / Maximal $\text{RFD}$ Rate of force development & peak power
Coaching / Sport Application

In explosive field sports (e.g., football, track and field throwing), structural power exercises should form the foundation of off-season and preseason programming. Single-joint assistance exercises should be appended at the end of sessions to maintain joint integrity without accumulating fatigue that impairs technical power execution.

pages.title: Part 2: Movement Analysis of the Sport: Sport-Specificity and Muscle Balance
pages.readingHtml:
Applying Biomechanical Relevance to Exercise Selection

To maximize training transfer, exercises selected for an athletic program must align with the movement analysis conducted during Step 1 (Needs Analysis). The closer a resistance training exercise mimics the movement patterns, joint angles, and muscular recruitment of the sporting action, the greater the positive adaptation transfer—a concept embodied by the Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demands (SAID) principle.

Sport-Specific Exercise Selection: Back Squat versus Leg Press

While multiple exercises can target identical prime movers, biomechanical posture and balance demands dictate athletic transfer. Consider an athlete training to improve vertical jump performance in basketball:

  • Primary Muscles: Vertical jumping requires rapid extension of the hip and knee joints, driven by the gluteus maximus, hamstrings, and quadriceps.
  • Leg Press Machine: Strengthening the hip and knee extensors in a seated, back-supported position removes postural balance, core stabilization, and axial weight-bearing forces.
  • Free Weight Back Squat: Strengthens the hip and knee extensors from an erect, standing position requiring active postural balance, ground reaction force application, and trunk rigidity.

Because jumping is performed from an upright body position under weight-bearing conditions, the back squat is far more sport-specific than the leg press and is strongly preferred. Incorporating explosive power exercises such as the power clean or snatch further enhances transfer by matching the fast rate of force development ($\text{RFD}$) inherent to jumping.

Muscle Balance and Agonist-Antagonist Ratios

While sport-specificity drives movement selection, programming exclusively for prime movers can create strength disparities across joints, elevating injury risk. Exercise selection must ensure proper muscle balance between opposing muscle groups:

  • Agonist: The muscle or muscle group actively causing the movement (e.g., the quadriceps during a leg extension exercise).
  • Antagonist: The muscle or muscle group located on the opposite side of the limb that acts passively or eccentrically to decelerate or stabilize the joint (e.g., the hamstrings during a leg extension exercise).
Defining Muscular Balance

Muscular balance does not imply a $1:1$ ratio of equal absolute strength between agonists and antagonists. Rather, it refers to a physiologically appropriate ratio of strength, power, or endurance tailored to joint mechanics (e.g., a normal functional hamstring-to-quadriceps strength ratio of approximately $0.60\text{--}0.75$). If isokinetic testing reveals an abnormal deficit (e.g., weak hamstrings relative to quadriceps in sprinters), targeted assistance exercises (e.g., Romanian deadlifts, leg curls) must be selected to restore balance and protect the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

Sport / Athletic Action Primary Movement Pattern Agonist Muscle Groups Sport-Specific Exercise Selection Antagonist / Balance Exercise
Basketball Vertical Jump Triple Extension (Hip/Knee/Ankle) Gluteals, Quadriceps, Gastrocnemius Back Squat, Power Clean, Push Jerk Romanian Deadlift, Hamstring Curl
Sprinter Acceleration Horizontal Driving & Knee Flexion Gluteals, Hamstrings, Quadriceps Power Clean, Barbell Lunge, Step-Up Leg Extension, Tibialis Anterior Raise
Baseball Overhand Pitch Internal Rotation & Shoulder Adduction Pectoralis Major, Latissimus Dorsi Bench Press, Lat Pulldown Dumbbell External Rotation, Face Pull
Coaching / Sport Application

Strength coaches should review program designs to ensure every pushing movement (e.g., bench press, overhead press) is paired with a corresponding pulling movement (e.g., bent-over row, chest-supported row) to maintain scapular stability and prevent glenohumeral impingement syndromes.

pages.title: Part 3: Athlete Experience, Equipment Availability, and Session Time Constraints
pages.readingHtml:
Operational and Practical Considerations in Exercise Selection

Beyond biomechanical and physiological requirements, exercise selection is heavily constrained by three operational factors: the athlete's exercise technique experience, the availability of training equipment, and the allocated workout time per session.

Exercise Technique Experience and Skill Progression

The strength and conditioning professional must evaluate the athlete's training status and technical proficiency. If an athlete's technique is questionable, the coach must observe a demonstration and provide complete instructional progression before assigning heavy loads:

  • Unskilled / Novice Athletes: Frequently introduced to resistance training using weight machines and free weight assistance exercises. These movements feature lower balance, coordination, and stabilization demands, allowing safer motor learning.
  • Advanced Athletes: Progress from basic machine movements to complex free weight structural and power lifts (e.g., front squat $\rightarrow$ hang power clean $\rightarrow$ power clean) as coordination and postural control improve.
  • Safety Rule: Never assume an athlete will perform an exercise correctly simply because the movement appears simple or is performed on a guided machine.

Availability of Resistance Training Equipment

Facility equipment constraints directly shape exercise selection. When preferred equipment is unavailable, strength coaches must select biomechanically equivalent substitutes:

  • Absence of Revolving-Sleeve Barbells: Performing explosive Olympic lifts (power clean, snatch) without Olympic barbells featuring smooth, revolving sleeves subjects the wrists and elbows to severe torque. In their absence, power lifts must be omitted or substituted with dumbbell high pulls or medicine ball throws.
  • Insufficient Weight Plate Inventory: If heavy barbell loads cannot be loaded due to plate shortages, coaches can substitute exercises that require less absolute external loading to achieve an equivalent relative muscular strain (e.g., replacing the heavy back squat with the single-leg split squat or front squat).

Available Training Time per Session

Strength coaches must constantly balance the sport-specific value of an exercise against the time required to set up and perform it:

Case Study: Time Efficiency vs. Sport Specificity

Consider selecting exercises for the hip and thigh extensors of a $100\text{ m}$ sprinter under strict session time limits:

  • Option A (Free Weight Barbell Lunge): Requires loading plates on both ends of a bar, securing spring collars, backing out of a rack, establishing balance, executing $10$ repetitions per leg ($20$ total reps), and reracking the bar.
  • Option B (Machine Leg Press): Requires adjusting a seat, inserting a selectorized weight stack pin, and executing $10$ repetitions in seconds.

Although the barbell lunge offers superior sport-specificity, selecting the leg press saves significant setup time. That saved time can be reallocated to perform additional sets or include supplementary assistance exercises, depending on seasonal priorities.

Exercises to Promote Recovery

At the conclusion of a high-intensity resistance training session, or during dedicated light microcycle sessions, coaches may prescribe recovery exercises. These consist of lightly loaded resistance movements or low-intensity aerobic exercises characterized by low muscular and neurological stress.

Physiological Mechanisms of Recovery Exercises:

  • Maintains active localized blood flow to exercised muscle tissue without inducing additional microtrauma.
  • Accelerates the clearance of metabolic byproducts and hydrogen ions ($\text{H}^+$).
  • Supplies oxygen and circulating amino acids to optimize muscle tissue repair and protein synthesis.
Operational Constraint Primary Limitation Coaching Adjustment / Modification Practical Trade-Off
Low Technique Experience Poor coordination & balance Assign machines & assistance exercises first Lower sport-specificity during learning phase
Lack of Revolving Barbells Wrist/elbow torque during catches Substitute DB high pulls or plyometric jumps Altered catching kinetics in Olympic lifts
Limited Plate Inventory Inability to reach heavy $1\text{RM}$ load Substitute single-leg squats or front squats Achieves high relative strain with lower absolute mass
Restricted Session Time Inability to perform long setups Prioritize selectorized machines & compound lifts Saves setup time to maintain total set volume

glossary.def: The process of choosing specific resistance training exercises for an athlete's program based on sport requirements, exercise technique experience, equipment availability, and training time.

Multijoint exercises that recruit one or more large muscle areas (e.g., chest, shoulder, back, hip, thigh) and receive high priority in program design due to their direct application to sport performance.

Single-joint exercises that recruit smaller muscle areas (e.g., upper arm, abdominal muscles, calf, neck, lower back) and are primarily used for injury prevention, muscular balance, or rehabilitation.
Core exercises that load the spine directly or indirectly, requiring postural muscular stabilization of a rigid torso and neutral spine during execution.
Structural exercises performed very quickly or explosively to maximize rate of force development and peak power output (e.g., power clean, snatch).
Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demands; the concept that the type of demand placed on the body dictates the nature of the physiological adaptation.
The primary muscle or muscle group actively causing a movement (e.g., quadriceps during knee extension).
The muscle or muscle group located on the opposite side of a joint that can passively lengthen or act to control movement (e.g., hamstrings during knee extension).
The proper relative ratio of strength, power, or muscular endurance between opposing muscle groups across a joint.

Lightly loaded resistance or low-intensity aerobic exercises performed to promote blood flow, remove metabolic byproducts, and enhance tissue repair without placing high stress on the muscular or nervous systems.
